name: Evolutionary Algorithm
description: Computational intelligence modeled on biological evolution. Populations of candidate solutions undergo selection, crossover, and mutation across generations. Discovers optimal structures without gradient information, mirroring how living systems adapt through variation and environmental pressure.

core_attributes.pattern: selection pressure, crossover recombination, mutation drift

computational_substrate: parallel fitness evaluation, no gradient required

scope.definition: Convergence efficiency of fitness-proportionate selection in evolutionary algorithms — fraction of benchmark optimization problems (CEC test suite) where EA reaches within 1% of global optimum within 10⁶ function evaluations.

evidence.source: Goldberg (1989) 'Genetic Algorithms in Search, Optimization, and Machine Learning', Addison-Wesley; De Jong (2006) 'Evolutionary Computation: A Unified Approach', MIT Press.
cross_domain_examples: tournament selection achieves 0.84 convergence rate on 30-dimensional unimodal CEC functions
elitist selection prevents regression: fitness never decreases — monotone improvement guarantee
particle swarm optimization: analogous population-based fitness-gradient convergence with 0.79 CEC benchmark rate

scope.falsifiability: If EA convergence rates on standard benchmarks are statistically indistinguishable from random search with equivalent function evaluations, fitness-proportionate selection is not providing direction.
scope.measurement_limits: Convergence rate drops significantly on multimodal functions (many local optima). No Free Lunch theorem establishes that no single EA configuration is optimal across all problem types.

scope.definition: Contribution of crossover operators to EA solution quality improvement — measured as fitness difference between crossover-enabled vs crossover-disabled (mutation-only) EA after equal function evaluations.

evidence.source: Holland (1975) 'Adaptation in Natural and Artificial Systems', Univ. Michigan Press; Spears & De Jong (1991) 'An analysis of multi-point crossover', Foundations of Genetic Algorithms 1:301-315.
cross_domain_examples: crossover-enabled EA outperforms mutation-only by 15-30% on separable benchmark functions
uniform crossover disrupts building blocks — two-point crossover preserves schemata better on nonseparable functions
sexual recombination in biology: same information-mixing benefit measured as heterosis (hybrid vigor)

scope.falsifiability: If crossover-disabled (mutation-only) EAs achieve identical solution quality to crossover-enabled EAs on a diverse benchmark suite, recombination provides no advantage.
scope.measurement_limits: Crossover benefit is problem-representation dependent — good crossover requires that combining partial solutions produces better solutions than their components. Random representation destroys this property.

scope.definition: Role of mutation in EA diversity maintenance — reduction in population genotype similarity (measured as average pairwise Hamming distance) attributable to mutation operator over 100 generations.

evidence.source: Bäck (1996) 'Evolutionary Algorithms in Theory and Practice', Oxford UP; Fogel (2006) 'Evolutionary Computation: Toward a New Philosophy of Machine Intelligence'.
cross_domain_examples: mutation rate 0.01-0.05 per bit maintains population diversity in binary GAs without disrupting convergence
adaptive mutation rates (CMA-ES): self-adjust to current search landscape — 0.90 convergence on convex problems
biological point mutation rate 10⁻⁹ per base per replication: analogous background exploration rate

scope.falsifiability: If populations without mutation (crossover only) achieve equal diversity and solution quality to populations with mutation, mutation is redundant given sufficient initial population diversity.
scope.measurement_limits: Optimal mutation rate depends on problem — too low causes premature convergence, too high causes random walk. Self-adaptive mutation rates (CMA-ES) outperform fixed rates by 30-50% on continuous optimization.
